question: What do we know about the generational wealth transfer, and how are these five preparing for it?

claims.text: The generational wealth transfer opportunity: Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) projects households will transfer $123.7 trillion to heirs ($105 trillion) and charities ($18 trillion) between now and 2048. UBS (published 2026-04-22) estimates USD 83 trillion in private wealth will change hands globally over the next two to three decades, the largest transfer of wealth in modern history.

Schwab: Schwab states (2025Q3) that client assets are more concentrated among older generations today, while the average age of its clients continues to get younger. Schwab reports (2026Q3) that roughly 75% of assets are retained in a wealth transfer event, that roughly 80% of retail assets are held by ultra-high net worth and high net worth households, and that its retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high and it is winning assets with all generations. Schwab states (2025Q4) the average age of its client has fallen by about 10 years in the last decade and is now in the 40s. Schwab cites industry research (2025Q3) that Gen Z is 45% more likely to start investing by age 21 as compared to Millennials. Schwab reports (2026Q3) that approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and Millennials, and (2024Q4) that 33% of new-to-firm retail households are under age 30 and more than 50% are under age 40. Schwab reports that 61% of new clients are Gen Z and Millennial investors.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones states (10-K 2025) that an aging client base is one of the demographic factors influencing elevated asset outflows and the downward trend in net new assets, and that the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer include changing client demographics, preferences and values, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs. Edward Jones identifies (10-K 2025) competition for clients and personnel in light of generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values as a strategic risk.

Industry research: Cerulli projects Generation Xers will inherit $39 trillion and Millennials will inherit $46 trillion; women in the Baby Boomer and older generations will receive $40 trillion in 'horizontal' transfers as they outlive their husbands, and women in younger generations will receive $47 trillion of the wealth transferred intergenerationally. Cerulli notes wealth is now more likely to be held by older households, and notes notable differences in service preferences among women and next-generation clients compared to current client demographics, likely to shift marketshare to firms best prepared. UBS attributes the wealth transfer to aging demographics, longer life expectancies, and decades of rising asset prices.

Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's strategic-update deck (2026) lists Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning and Founders Wealth Strategies among capabilities provided across clients' growth cycles, under the Preserve Wealth and Invest for the Future stages. CEO Ted Pick stated (2025Q4) the firm is using its scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors, including family office and OCIO, as part of retaining and serving wealthy clients.

Schwab: Schwab states (2026-09-30) its retail business is built to win across generations, that its retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high, and that roughly 80% of retail assets are held by ultra-high net worth and high net worth households, positioning it to serve future generations when wealth is passed on. Schwab reports (2026Q3) approximately 75% of assets are retained in a wealth transfer event. Schwab is enhancing its tax, trust, and estate capabilities, including plans to offer Wealth.com's estate planning tools to retail clients (2025-06-30); it made a strategic investment in Wealth.com (2025-03-31), took an ownership stake and began rolling out estate analysis capability to specialists (2025-12-31), and increased its investment to bring AI-powered estate planning tools to clients with plans to launch AI-powered tax planning (2026-03-31).

Edward Jones: The Partnership states (10-K 2025) its new-client initiatives include a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, alongside High Net Worth and Workplace initiatives; it seeks to address strategic risks including competition for clients and personnel in light of generational wealth transfer through initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact; and Business Resource Group members and colleagues come together to discover ways to serve clients and future clients more deeply as demographics and needs change.

Raymond James: Raymond James's private wealth buildout (trade press, 2026-09-29) includes estate and charitable planning capabilities, lending and cash management solutions, risk management services, and intergenerational wealth strategies. Its Private Wealth Advisor designation program, launched in September 2022, provides training, coaching, and a peer network for advisors specializing in high-net-worth clients (generally at least $5 million in investable assets); as of September 2026 nearly 450 advisors had earned the designation.

Schwab: Schwab's financial consultant career achievement plan (FY2025) is a noncontributory, unfunded, nonqualified retirement plan under which an eligible financial consultant receives earned cash payments after retirement, contingent upon meeting performance levels, tenure, age, and client transitioning requirements; full vesting occurs at age 60 with at least ten years of service. Schwab's Advisor Services segment (FY2025) offers advisors help to establish independent practices with access to business start-up and transition consultants, technology engineers, and dedicated service teams. Schwab noted it has some 3,000 in-house financial advisors, many holding CFPs, and plans to hire thousands more financial consultants to serve retail investors across its 400 branches.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones states (10-K 2025) eligible retiring financial advisors are offered individually tailored retirement transition plans, compensating a retiring advisor for client transition services under an agreement generally running five years (two years as employee providing transition services, then retirement and a three-year non-compete). Edward Jones reported financial advisor attrition of 6.4% in 2025Q2 (primarily due to an increase in retirements) and 6.1% in 2025Q3 (including a rise in departures with tenure of five years or less). Edward Jones maintains (10-K 2025) a comprehensive onboarding program for financial advisors, and all general partners, including the Managing Partner and ELT, must retire as general partners by the end of the calendar year in which they turn age 65.

Merrill: Merrill develops the next generation of advisors through its Advisor Development Program (ADP), which trains new advisors through progressive roles (ADP Client Associate, ADP Financial Solutions Advisor, ADP Financial Advisor) until they graduate to Merrill Core Advisor. Merrill continues to attract talent across both new and experienced advisers (2026-03-31), runs a training program viewed as the key driver to improve net new flows (2025-12-31), and approximately one-third of net new households in Q2 2025 were added by newly trained advisors. Merrill had 446 advisors named to the 2025 Forbes 'Top Next-Generation Wealth Advisors Best-in-State' list, which recognizes advisors born in 1986 or later.

Raymond James: Raymond James states (10-K 2025) it seeks to mitigate risks from retiring financial advisors through financial advisor succession planning and by providing advisors a broad range of services and resources; generally, with planned retirements, assets are retained at the firm pursuant to advisor succession plans. Raymond James provides succession and acquisition guidance to independent advisors and offers Succession Planning and Acquisition support to independent RIAs that custody with it. It lists a 'Next gen advisor strategy' among Private Client Group recruiting initiatives, and develops future advisors through its Wealth Management Associate Program and Advisor Mastery Program. Its 2025 RIA Benchmarking Survey found RIA principals increasingly have documented, long-term succession plans (a 40% improvement from 2023) and 87% have a catastrophic event plan.

Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's strategic presentation lists capabilities to serve clients throughout their growth cycle, including Founders Wealth Strategies, Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning, and Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits; capabilities to help founders and early-stage/private companies unlock liquidity, including Private Shares Trading & Lending and IPO Execution and Support Services; an expanded partnership with Carta offering advice-based services to founders and family offices; an EquityZen acquisition and Zero Hash collaboration framed as widening competitive moats; broadening capabilities for financial advisors including alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending; a more democratized offering of alternatives (e.g. evergreen products and lower denomination size) to its retail client base; and investments in E*TRADE, the self-directed channel, and workplace product as part of its client acquisition funnel.

Schwab: Schwab supports newer investors with accessible products such as Schwab Stock Slices and the Schwab Starter Kit, plus trading capabilities, advisory solutions and educational resources. Schwab lists the Schwab Starter Kit and Schwab Teen Investor Account with no/low commissions for younger investors, and offers the Schwab Teen Investor Account (2026-03-31). Schwab's crypto offering (2025-09-30) is positioned in part to appeal to young investors, and it offers young investors support, service, education, and its thinkorswim platform; 42% of thinkorswim users are Millennial or Gen Z. Schwab offers Schwab Crypto (retail Bitcoin and Ethereum trading, from May 2026) and is investing in AI-driven capabilities including the Investor AI Assistant, generative AI search, and AI learning & coaching within thinkorswim.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones states (10-K 2025) its initiatives include a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors; recently launched Financial Planning Services; High Net Worth (attracting and serving high net worth clients); and Workplace (connecting local business owners and their employees with financial solutions). Per trade press (2026-08-18), Edward Jones took a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, intended as a step toward integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities to support its value proposition and advisor conversations.

Merrill: Merrill announced (2026-09-15) the launch of Tax Efficient Transition Service (TET) and Dollar Cost Averaging Service (DCA), combining automation with professional portfolio oversight to help clients simplify asset transitions and cash deployment into managed or custom managed investment strategies; TET is designed for clients holding appreciated securities, and DCA for clients holding cash balances. Merrill offers robust solutions for ultra-high-net-worth clients including alternative investments and sustainable and impact investing strategies. At Merrill Lynch, client sales of alternative investments increased 19% in 2026Q3, and Merrill/GWIM benefits from AI-enabled tools to help advisers prepare for client conversations; 81% of eligible brokerage and bank accounts were opened through digital onboarding in 2026Q3.

Raymond James: Raymond James's private wealth platform includes estate and charitable planning capabilities, lending and cash management solutions, risk management services, and intergenerational wealth strategies. It offers a Private Wealth Advisor designation program (launched September 2022) for advisors specializing in high-net-worth clients (generally at least $5 million in investable assets); Private Wealth Guided Portfolios combining equity and fixed income with a dedicated alternatives sleeve; and a Private Wealth offering plus a newly launched Business Owner & Workplace Solutions offering to support advisors serving business owners.

Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's integrated firm model is positioned to serve clients through their growth cycles, with Founders Wealth Strategies, full-service wealth advice and asset allocation plus Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning; it highlights Family Office, OCIO and Tailored Lending as offerings, offers family office infrastructure solutions for ultra-high net worth clients, and does substantial work to service founders and family offices. Morgan Stanley at Work positions the firm as an early trusted advisor to private companies and their employees, and the integrated firm lets a founder's wealth manager work with the investment banker across generations of wealth needs.
Schwab: Schwab's investor deck (2026Q3) is titled 'Built to win across generations' and reports approximately 75% of assets are retained in a wealth transfer event.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones (10-K 2025) includes among its new-client initiatives a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors; identifies generational wealth transfer as an evolving force that may adversely impact its ability to compete and adapt its business model; and seeks to address strategic risks including competition for clients and personnel in light of generational wealth transfer through initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact.

Merrill: Bank of America Private Bank, together with Merrill Wealth Management's Private Wealth Management business, provides customized solutions to meet clients' wealth structuring, investment management, trust and banking needs, including specialty asset management services. Merrill ranks No. 1 in Managed Personal Trust AUM and Bank of America was named Best Private Bank in the U.S. and Best Private Bank for Philanthropic Services Globally. Merrill advisors are supported by infrastructure enabling lead generation through Bank of America's global bank and trust division, with access to Bank of America's banking and trust capabilities.

Raymond James: Raymond James positions estate and charitable planning, lending and cash management, risk management, and intergenerational wealth strategies as tools advisors can draw on serving households with complex financial profiles; offers Private Wealth to help advisors serve high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth families; and provides RIA principals with succession planning and acquisition support. CEO Paul Shoukry states advisors build deeply personal relationships knowing the client's spouse and family and financial objectives, and describes Raymond James' culture as built on putting people first and earning trust over generations.

Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's strategic deck (2026) describes the integrated firm as delivering capabilities throughout clients' growth cycles, including Founders Wealth Strategies, Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning, Preserve Wealth, Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation, and Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits. CEO Ted Pick stated the firm is focused on both public and private ecosystems, augmented by the EquityZen acquisition, to cover growth companies and their employees from founding to public maturity. CFO Sharon Yeshaya explained the firm understands the full cap table and can convert IPO stock into advice-based relationships across the cap table, and described the exclusive Carta partnership referring private companies to Morgan Stanley as they go public. CEO Ted Pick described Solium as a 'hidden gem' acquisition to help transform where the firm is going with clients, and stated investments in self-directed and Workplace channels drive the firm's client acquisition funnel (over 19 million relationships, over $250 billion of net new assets annually). Why it might matter: CEO Ted Pick framed these workplace and self-directed investments as driving the differentiated client acquisition funnel 'on track to delivering $10 trillion plus of total client assets.'

Schwab: CEO Rick Wurster stated (2026-09-30) Schwab's retail business is built to win across generations and is well positioned to continue serving future generations when wealth is passed on, with an extremely high retention rate around wealth transfers. Why it might matter: Schwab's deck frames the firm's 'Built to win across generations' position with attract (~70% NTF retail households Gen Z & Millennials), serve (80% retail assets held by U/HNW households) and retain (~75% assets retained in a wealth transfer event) metrics. Schwab's deck (2026Q3) presents approximately 75% of assets retained in a wealth transfer event. Why it might matter: Schwab's total client assets reached $11.90 trillion at December 31, 2025, up 18% on the year, providing the asset base on which that retention acts. Schwab reports approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and Millennials (2026-09-30), and 80% of retail assets are held by ultra-high net worth and high net worth households. Why it might matter: Schwab states that 33% of new-to-firm retail households were under age 30 and more than 50% under age 40 in 2024Q4, indicating a younger incoming client base. Schwab is enhancing tax, trust and estate capabilities including plans to offer Wealth.com's estate planning tools (2025-06-30), made a strategic investment in Wealth.com (2025-03-31), took an ownership stake and rolled out estate analysis capability (2025-12-31), and increased its investment to bring AI-powered estate planning and, later, tax planning to clients (2026-03-31). Why it might matter: Schwab's CEO said the firm took these steps to give more tools to help clients integrate estate planning into their investment life. Why it might matter: the source does not say.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones states (10-K 2025) it is actively pursuing and making substantial investments in initiatives, including High Net Worth, Workplace, and a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors. Why it might matter: Edward Jones frames these initiatives as part of addressing strategic risks including competition for clients and personnel in light of generational wealth transfer. Edward Jones identifies generational wealth transfer as a risk to its continued ability to compete and notes significant investments in advisors, technology, digital initiatives, and data-powered tools to support long-term growth. Why it might matter: Edward Jones notes clients can transfer their business to competing organizations at any time. Edward Jones states it seeks to address strategic risks through initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact and makes significant investments to attract and retain qualified talent. Why it might matter: Edward Jones announced a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken as a step toward integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities.

Merrill: Merrill announced (2026-09-15) the launch of Tax Efficient Transition Service (TET) and Dollar Cost Averaging Service (DCA) to help clients simplify asset transitions and cash deployment into managed or custom managed investment strategies. Why it might matter: Merrill's Head of Managed Account Advisors, John Capelli, stated TET and DCA create more opportunities for meaningful client engagement. Merrill was recognized more than any other firm, with 446 advisors named to the 2025 Forbes 'Top Next-Generation Wealth Advisors Best-in-State' list. Why it might matter: the Forbes list considers 'next-gen' advisors to be those born in 1986 or later with a minimum of four years as an advisor. CFO Alastair Borthwick stated Merrill is picking up recruiting of experienced advisors and running a training program in wealth management to drive net new flows. Why it might matter: approximately one-third of net new households in Q2 2025 were added by newly trained advisors. Trade press reports (2026-11-16) recruited assets to the wealth unit doubled year-over-year as Merrill returned to veteran broker recruiting under Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf. Why it might matter: Merrill executives attributed the increase to a restored focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer.

Raymond James: Raymond James's private wealth buildout includes estate and charitable planning, lending and cash management, risk management, and intergenerational wealth strategies as tools advisors can draw on serving households with complex financial profiles; it launched its Private Wealth Advisor designation program in September 2022, with nearly 450 advisors earning the designation as of September 2026; and it lists a 'Next gen advisor strategy' among its recruiting initiatives. Why it might matter: Private Client Group President Tash Elwyn said 'we're committed to being a destination for private wealth advisors and the clients they serve.' Raymond James launched Private Wealth Guided Portfolios, integrating traditional and alternative investments within risk-based portfolios for high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients; and states it mitigates the risk of retiring advisors through financial advisor succession planning. Why it might matter: Raymond James states that, generally, with planned retirements, assets are retained at the firm pursuant to advisor succession plans. CEO Paul Shoukry attributed Raymond James' long-term results to 'the strength of a culture built on putting people first and earning trust over generations.' Why it might matter: the source does not say.

There is no single shared metric across the five firms on which to render a valid, evidence-based ranking of readiness. Each firm reports different evidence of preparedness: Morgan Stanley on integrated-firm capabilities (Founders Wealth Strategies, Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning, and IPO/cap-table capture) plus a 99% client retention figure and 60% of advisor-led assets with ~20-year relationship duration; Schwab on a 'Built to win across generations' framework with ~75% assets retained in wealth transfer events, ~70% of new-to-firm households being Gen Z/Millennial, and ~80% of retail assets held by U/HNW households; Edward Jones on documented risk and initiatives (a digital platform for Next Generation investors, High Net Worth, Workplace), but with net new asset declines attributed in part to generational wealth transfers outside the firm; Merrill on next-generation advisor development (446 Forbes Top Next-Gen advisors, No. 1 ranking) and asset-transition services (TET/DCA); and Raymond James on intergenerational wealth strategies, advisor succession planning, and a Private Wealth Advisor designation program (nearly 450 advisors). These are not directly comparable because the firms disclose different metrics, definitions, periods and scopes (for instance, net-new-asset and client-balance definitions differ across firms, and no common figure such as a wealth-transfer retention rate is disclosed by all five); an unverified or absent common basis means no single firm can be ranked most prepared on this evidence.

adjacent.text: Schwab: Schwab's investor day materials present a '$37 Trillion Opportunity' representing total U.S. retail channel assets, within which Schwab's Advisor Services holds $5.2 trillion.
adjacent.differs_because: The passage labels the figure as '$37 Trillion Opportunity' under a slide titled 'Total U.S. Retail Channel Assets,' which is a stock measure of current U.S. retail channel assets, not the generational wealth transfer (a flow of wealth transferring between generations) that the sub-question asks about.

adjacent.text: Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley defines Wealth Management net new assets as client asset inflows, inclusive of interest, dividends and asset acquisitions, less client asset outflows, excluding the impact of business combinations/divestitures and fees and commissions. Morgan Stanley's total client assets across Wealth and Investment Management grew to $9.3 trillion at year-end 2025 and stood at $10 trillion in 2026Q2; its Wealth Management total client assets stood at $8 trillion in 2026Q2 and $8.4 trillion in 2026Q3. Morgan Stanley reported full-year net new assets of $356.3 billion (2025) and $251.7 billion (2024), and quarterly net new assets of $122.3 billion (2025Q4), $118 billion (2026Q1), $148 billion (2026Q2), and $232 billion (2026Q3). Morgan Stanley stated it retains 99% of its clients, with 60% of advisor-led assets associated with clients averaging 20 years of relationship duration.
adjacent.differs_because: Net new assets and total/retained client assets are stand-in figures; they are not themselves a measure of wealth-transfer capture or generational asset retention.

adjacent.text: Schwab: Schwab states it retains approximately 75% of assets in a wealth transfer event, and its CEO states the retention rate around wealth transfers is extremely high. Schwab's total client assets reached $11.90 trillion at December 31, 2025, $10.10 trillion at year-end 2024, and $13.08 trillion at June 30, 2026. Core net new assets totaled $366.9 billion in 2024, $519.4 billion in 2025, $119.8 billion in 2026Q2, and $190.4 billion in 2026Q3.
adjacent.differs_because: Client assets and core net new assets are stand-in figures; only the ~75% wealth-transfer retention metric directly addresses transfer capture, and total client assets is a stock of balances rather than a transfer-specific measure.

adjacent.text: Edward Jones: Edward Jones ended 2025 with client assets under care (AUC) of $2.5 trillion (including $1.1 trillion advisory programs AUC) and 20,425 financial advisors; reported net new assets of $74 billion for 2025 (flat vs 2024) and $18 billion in 2026Q1 and 2026Q2; ended 2026Q1 with $2,417 billion total AUC and 6.8 million client households, and 2026Q2 with $2.6 trillion AUC (including $1.2 trillion advisory programs AUC). Edward Jones reported financial advisor attrition of 6.4% (2025Q2) and 6.1% (2025Q3), and attributed net-new-asset declines to an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm.
adjacent.differs_because: Net new assets and client AUC are stand-in figures for retention/capture, and advisor attrition is a workforce metric rather than a measure of wealth-transfer capture.

adjacent.text: Merrill: Merrill (GWIM, including Merrill and the Private Bank) reported total client balances of $4,751,394 million at December 31, 2025, $4.9 trillion at June 30, 2026, and $5,056,787 million at September 30, 2026 (climbing above $5 trillion for the first time); Merrill Wealth Management client balances were $4,240,601 million and Bank of America Private Bank $816,186 million at September 30, 2026. Net client AUM flows (GWIM) were $20,209 million (2025Q4), $20,372 million (2026Q1), $13,673 million (2026Q2), and $19,980 million (2026Q3). Merrill added about 4,200 net new households with at least $500,000 in assets in 2026Q3, and the Private Bank added about 470 net new relationships with at least $3 million under management in 2026Q3. Merrill reported adviser attrition is near historic lows (2026Q2).
adjacent.differs_because: Client balances and net client AUM flows are stand-in figures for retention/capture; net household additions are a lead-generation metric, and none directly measure wealth-transfer capture. GWIM figures cover Merrill plus Bank of America Private Bank, not Merrill alone.

adjacent.text: Raymond James: Raymond James reported Private Client Group client assets under administration of $1.54 trillion (2025-03-31), $1.57 trillion (2025-06-30), and $1.67 trillion (2025-09-30); whole-firm client assets under administration of $1.77 trillion (2025-12-31), $1.76 trillion (2026-03-31), and $1.92 trillion (2026-06-30). Domestic Private Client Group net new assets were $8.8 billion (2025-03-31), $11.7 billion (2025-06-30), nearly $18 billion (2025-09-30), $30.8 billion (2025-12-31), $23.0 billion (2026-03-31), and $21.7 billion (2026-06-30). Raymond James noted domestic financial advisor retention remained very strong for FY2025, and historically experienced about 1% regretted attrition.
adjacent.differs_because: Client assets under administration and domestic net new assets are stand-in figures for retention/capture; advisor retention is a workforce metric rather than a measure of wealth-transfer capture.
